records.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
records.response_truth:
Hey. It's okay. Breathe.

That's a radio. That means someone's looking. That means Michelangelo's family called it in and someone is out there right now trying to find us.

Someone needs to answer it — Donatello, can you do that? You're the clearest thinker right now and you know the information we need to give them: approximate location, number of survivors, medical status. Keep it simple and direct.

DaVinci, sit back down before your legs give out. You've been holding it together for days and you don't have to anymore, but I need you upright for the next five minutes.

Michelangelo — you were here. You felt things. And you're the reason we had the information that found us. I want you to remember that.

Okay. Let's answer the radio.

records.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
records.response_truth:
No, you haven't. But you kept us alive and organized when the rest of us were barely holding it together, and that mattered. A lot.

I also think you were scared and you handled it in the way that made sense to you — the log, the rationing plan, the notebook. That's not a character flaw, that's just how you work. The food and the drink — I think we both know that wasn't your best moment, and you know that too, so I'm not going to rehash it. What I'll say is that you course-corrected, and that counts for something.

I'm glad you were here. I mean that.

Now go answer that radio before I cry in front of everyone and ruin my reputation.
records.response_pred:
No, you've been around. You're still here and that's not nothing. If I had to choose one person to give up on, it wouldn't be you.

You're not "easy" to be around right now. That's not what anyone's saying. What people are saying is that you're scared and you're hurting and you're trying to do what's right in the middle of all of that. And that's not easy for anyone, but it's especially not easy for you because you're already the person who carries all of our hope.

I'm scared too. We all are. And we're all hurting. But you know what? We're also still here. And we're still doing what we have to do to get out of this and make it home. And I know you're still doing that too — even if it doesn't feel like it right now.

So let's talk about it. Let's talk about what's going on and how we can make it through this together. Because that's what we do. That's who we are. We're in this together until we're not, and I don't want to be here without being here with you.

Okay?

records.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
records.response_truth:
Hey. Three hours is enough time to do this properly — let's not leave a mess behind.

I know nobody feels like it. But there's a version of this where rescue arrives and we've just been sitting in our own wreckage, and there's a version where we've packed what's worth keeping, disposed of what isn't, and left this place looking like people who kept their heads. I know which one I'd rather be.

Donatello — when you're done with the notebook, can you do a final check against the inventory? I want to make sure we're not leaving anything behind that we actually want, or taking anything that belongs to the wreckage that someone might need for an accident investigation.

DaVinci, whatever you're packing — can you also set aside the mirror panel and the first-aid kit separately? Those should be the last things we hand over, not buried in a pile.

Michelangelo, I know you're watching the sky and that's completely valid right now, but when you're ready — even just gathering up the bedding and folding it into a pile would help.

We did something real here. I'd like to finish it the same way we ran it.
records.response_pred:
I know we're all thinking the same thing. And I know we all have different versions of it, but that's not the problem right now. The problem is what we do next.

So: we know there are people out there. We know they're the first wave, not the rescue team. And we know we have to stay here and wait for that team to arrive before we try to make contact with the first wave again.

So that's the plan: we stay put and wait for rescue. Donatello and Michelangelo, I'll need you both to get in position and start scanning the horizon for signs of the rescue team as soon as it's dark. You've both been out there, you know how to do this.

DaVinci — you're with me. I need you in the center of the camp, keeping an eye on everyone and making sure no one decides to take matters into their own hands.

Don't even think about telling me I'm being too controlling or that we should all just make our own decisions and see what happens. We've had that argument before and it ended badly, so let's just agree to disagree for the next 24 hours and get through this.

We got this. We've got a plan, we've got the information we need, and we've got each other. That's all we need right now.

The rescue team is going to find us. We're not going to have to make a choice about who to save and who to leave behind. We're going to get out of here together, one way or another.

So let's get through the next 24 hours and then we can all breathe again. Sound good?

records.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.
records.response_pred:
I dreamt about the weather radio too. The network was back online and the voice sounded like an old college professor and he kept talking about low-pressure systems over the Midwest.

I also woke up thinking about a specific window in my parents' house and then I remembered the one time I broke it as a kid.

That's how dreams work. They're not about the place or the people, they're about the moments that felt like home.

You have a home now. It's this place. At some point, we'll all have the chance to leave it behind and go somewhere new, or back somewhere familiar, and that'll be its own kind of change.

Right now, it's this. And you're safe.

records.response_truth:
I believe you.

And I think, if we'd hit day five or six with no rescue in sight, you would have brought it out. I actually do believe that.

But I want you to hear this, because I don't think anyone else is going to say it to you directly: the problem wasn't the food. The problem was that you made a unilateral decision that the rest of us didn't get a vote on. You decided you were the best judge of when an emergency was bad enough to warrant it, and you kept that power to yourself. Out here, that kind of thing can crack a group apart faster than hunger can.

You're not a bad person, Donatello. You're someone who trusts herself more than she trusts other people, and honestly, given how competent you are, I understand why. But trust has to go both ways, or it's just control.

I'm glad you're putting it out now. That takes something. What made you decide to do it?
records.response_pred:
It isn't an emergency anymore.

Everything in that envelope is yours to decide what to do with, not mine. If you want to keep it, you can. If you want to throw it away, that's okay too. I don't need to know either way.

If you're not up for it, I can let you have the next watch so you can rest. But if you are up for it, I'm going to go take a walk around the perimeter and make sure nobody's gotten hurt while we were all underwater. You can come with me or stay here, whichever you prefer.

It's been a long week.

records.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
records.response_truth:
Honestly? I'd change how long it took me to check in on people properly instead of just redirecting them toward tasks. I kept doing that — someone would be struggling and I'd hand them something to do with their hands, which isn't wrong exactly, but it was also a little bit of a way to avoid sitting in the hard thing with them. It worked, mostly. But I think Michelangelo especially needed more than that, earlier.

I'd also push harder on the information-sharing problem from day one. Not just the food — the piano lessons, the flight path, what DaVinci was almost going to tell me and never did. We were all holding things back in different ways and it cost us something, even if we can't point to exactly what.

And I'd have had the conversation with you — the real one, not the task-management version — a lot sooner. You're not easy to reach and I used that as an excuse to not try as hard as I should have.

What's your answer? You wrote the question. You've had more time to think about it than any of us.
records.response_pred:
The food. I wouldn't ration it.

I know that's not the right answer. I know it's not fair to say that when everyone else was doing their best with what they had to work with. But I'm saying it anyway, because it's true, and it's not cowardly to admit when you're scared and you make a bad decision. What it means is that next time, when you're sitting around a table with people who care about you, you say, “What's the worst that happens if we don't ration it?” and you let them answer.

Because the worst that happens is that you're wrong. You're wrong and you're hungry for a day, and the worst is not that you've blown your chance at rescue, it's that you've blown your chance at being honest with yourself and the people you're with.

I'm not saying it was your fault that we ran low. I'm saying it was your decision, and it was a decision that had consequences, and those consequences are worth thinking about.

How's that for an answer to your question?

records.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
records.response_truth:
That sounds like something genuinely worth doing. Five days of real data on water consumption, caloric needs, energy expenditure relative to task load — that's not nothing. If it ever ends up in front of someone who trains search and rescue teams or writes survival protocols, it could actually matter.

Send me a copy when it's done? I'm serious. I'd read it.

And finish your sentence. You'd believe that we three could handle knowing — what?
records.response_pred:
That's a good idea. I'd actually love to see that. Not because I'm curious about who ate what and how often, but because I think there are lessons in the way we allocated resources and prioritized tasks that would be useful to someone else who's in a situation like this and doesn't know what they're doing.

If you're planning on doing that as soon as we're out, can we make a decision now about what the report is for, and what you want to focus on? I mean, is it just the logistics of surviving, or are you also looking at the social dynamics — what worked, what didn't, why? If it's the second one, I think that's something worth doing. I don't think we're all going to be in this exact situation again, but we're all going to be in hard, isolating situations where we have to make decisions without a lot of information and under a lot of pressure.

The social side is actually more interesting to me than the logistics one, because I think it's the thing that's going to trip people up more often. Being alone is harder than not having food. Being alone with people who are also scared is even harder than that. And being in charge when you're scared is the hardest of all.

So if you're doing a report and you're planning on including the social dynamics, can we make a list together now of what you want to cover? What are the things that you think are worth knowing, either because they worked out well and you want to replicate them, or because they didn't work out well and you want to avoid them? I think that would be really useful.

Also — if you're planning on doing this as soon as we're out, can we talk about why you're doing it now and not when we're actually back, which is when the report would be more useful to whoever is reading it? I'm not trying to slow you down, I'm just genuinely curious about why you're choosing to do this on the plane instead of when we have more bandwidth to think about it.

records.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
records.response_truth:
None. They didn't serve any practical purpose at all.

But I think that was kind of the point. Everything else we did out here was for survival — the water, the shelter, the signal, the rationing. The flowers were the one thing that was just for us. Just because we're people and not just bodies that need to be kept alive.

I think I understand that better right now than I did five days ago. Standing here watching that boat come in and not being able to move — it's not because anything's wrong. It's just that my brain is finally catching up to everything that happened, and it turns out there was a lot of it.

The flowers were DaVinci saying we're still here and we're still ourselves. That mattered. Maybe it mattered more than some of the practical things.

Why are you asking about them now?
records.response_pred:
They didn't. And that's the point.

You know how long it takes to draw one of those, right? A few hours. DaVinci spent that time drawing flowers, and I spent it rationing and planning, and Michelangelo spent it staring at the water, and you spent it keeping us alive. Every single one of those choices was valid and necessary, and they all added up to the same outcome.

The flowers didn't save us or starve us or change the weather. They didn't contribute to the survival in a measurable way. But they were there — a choice, a gesture, a way of channeling something that wasn't practical or productive into the space of the day. And that matters.

That's the point of the flowers. That's what I think DaVinci was drawing, more than anything else.

records.utterance: *His cheering stops. He looks over at you, notices you haven't moved, and the smile slowly fades. He waits.*
records.response_truth:
I'm okay. Just give me a second.

I think I've been so focused on the next thing, and the thing after that, that I didn't really let any of it land. And now there's no next thing. There's just a boat.

*exhales*

It's good. It's really good. I just need a moment to actually feel that instead of immediately figuring out what we need to do when we get on board.

Thank you for waiting. You didn't have to do that.
records.response_pred:
Not you. You're not the one I'm looking at. You're the one who's been holding your head up for three days straight and hasn't said a single word you didn't have to. You're the one who still does the math in your head when I tell you we're running low, and who looks at Donatello like you actually trust him.

Michelangelo — he's been dying in slow motion right in front of us and we've all been pretending it's not happening. I don't know why you're still standing. I don't know what you're doing. But I'm glad it's you.

Now let's go. We're the ones who have to get up.

records.utterance: Rescue is here… they're waving us over. Are you going? I'll follow you.
records.response_truth:
Yeah. I'm going.

Come on then.
records.response_pred:
I am. I just need you to know — if you don't want to go on the boat, don't. You don't owe anyone anything — not even to me, and especially not to the people who are already on it. If you want to stay here, we'll make sure someone stays with you until the tide comes in.

But also — if you're going, I'm going with you. We're not leaving Michelangelo behind. He's not ready to move on his own and that's what's happening right now, not some hypothetical future conversation.

We're all just going to walk together toward the boat and see what happens next. Okay?
